subject: River Otter
fact: River otters are excellent swimmers and can close their ears and nostrils underwater.

subject: Beaver
fact: Beavers build dams that can create ponds and wetland habitats.

subject: Muskrat
fact: Muskrats build homes from mud and wetland plants.

subject: American Mink
fact: Minks are strong swimmers that often hunt near streams and wetlands.

subject: Capybara
fact: Capybaras are the world's largest rodents and spend lots of time near water.

subject: Nutria
fact: Nutria are large semi-aquatic rodents with orange front teeth.

subject: Water Vole
fact: Water voles live along slow-moving streams, ponds, and riverbanks.

subject: Marsh Rabbit
fact: Marsh rabbits are strong swimmers that live around wetlands.

subject: Hippopotamus
fact: Hippos spend much of the day in water to stay cool.

subject: Pygmy Hippo
fact: Pygmy hippos live around forest streams and swamps in West Africa.

subject: Manatee
fact: Manatees are gentle plant-eating mammals that graze on aquatic vegetation.

subject: Amazon River Dolphin
fact: Amazon river dolphins can turn their necks more than ocean dolphins can.

subject: Ganges River Dolphin
fact: Ganges river dolphins use echolocation to navigate muddy river water.

subject: Giant Otter
fact: Giant otters live in family groups and communicate with many different calls.

subject: Platypus
fact: Platypuses use sensitive bills to find food underwater.

subject: American Alligator
fact: Alligators can create water-filled holes that help other wetland animals during dry periods.

subject: American Crocodile
fact: American crocodiles can live in both fresh and salty water habitats.

subject: Freshwater Crocodile
fact: Freshwater crocodiles are smaller and slimmer than saltwater crocodiles.

subject: Gharial
fact: Gharials have long narrow snouts that are well suited for catching fish.

subject: Common Snapping Turtle
fact: Snapping turtles have powerful jaws and spend much of their lives in water.

subject: Painted Turtle
fact: Painted turtles often bask together on logs in the sun.

subject: Softshell Turtle
fact: Softshell turtles have flattened shells covered by leathery skin.

subject: Map Turtle
fact: Map turtles have fine shell markings that can look like lines on a map.

subject: Red-Eared Slider
fact: Red-eared sliders are named for the red markings behind their eyes.

subject: Green Anaconda
fact: Green anacondas are heavy-bodied snakes that spend lots of time in water.

subject: Water Moccasin
fact: Water moccasins are venomous snakes often found around southeastern wetlands.

subject: Northern Water Snake
fact: Northern water snakes are nonvenomous and often swim with their bodies near the surface.

subject: Green Frog
fact: Green frogs live around ponds, streams, and marshes.

subject: Bullfrog
fact: Bullfrogs are large frogs with deep calls that can sound like a low bellow.

subject: Leopard Frog
fact: Leopard frogs have dark spots on their backs and strong jumping legs.

subject: Tree Frog
fact: Many tree frogs have sticky toe pads that help them climb vegetation.

subject: Newt
fact: Newts are amphibians that often spend part of their lives in water.

subject: Mudpuppy
fact: Mudpuppies are fully aquatic salamanders with feathery external gills.

subject: Axolotl
fact: Axolotls keep their larval features and external gills as adults.

subject: Great Blue Heron
fact: Great blue herons stand still in shallow water before striking at prey.

subject: Great Egret
fact: Great egrets use long necks and sharp bills to catch fish and other small animals.

subject: Green Heron
fact: Green herons sometimes drop small objects on water as bait to attract fish.

subject: Roseate Spoonbill
fact: Roseate spoonbills sweep their spoon-shaped bills side to side through shallow water.

subject: Wood Stork
fact: Wood storks find prey by touch as they move their open bills through the water.

subject: Sandhill Crane
fact: Sandhill cranes perform elaborate dances with jumps and wing flaps.

subject: Common Moorhen
fact: Moorhens use long toes to walk over floating vegetation.

subject: Purple Gallinule
fact: Purple gallinules have very long toes for walking on lily pads and marsh plants.

subject: Mallard
fact: Mallards tip forward in shallow water to reach plants and small animals below the surface.

subject: Wood Duck
fact: Wood ducks often nest in tree cavities near water.

subject: Canada Goose
fact: Canada geese commonly rest and feed around lakes, rivers, and wetlands.

subject: Belted Kingfisher
fact: Kingfishers dive headfirst into water to catch fish.

subject: Osprey
fact: Ospreys have special gripping feet that help them hold slippery fish.

subject: Bald Eagle
fact: Bald eagles often hunt fish near rivers and lakes.

subject: River Kingfisher
fact: Many kingfishers perch above water and watch for fish before diving.

subject: Common Loon
fact: Loons are powerful divers with legs positioned far back on their bodies.

subject: Bluegill
fact: Bluegills are freshwater sunfish commonly found in ponds and slow rivers.

subject: Largemouth Bass
fact: Largemouth bass are ambush predators with very large mouths.

subject: Channel Catfish
fact: Channel catfish use whisker-like barbels to sense food in murky water.

subject: Common Carp
fact: Carp use sensitive barbels near their mouths to help search for food.

subject: Alligator Gar
fact: Alligator gar have long bodies, armored scales, and broad toothy jaws.

subject: Fallfish
fact: Fallfish are large minnows that live in clear rivers and streams.

subject: Crayfish
fact: Crayfish use claws to grab food and defend themselves.

subject: Freshwater Mussel
fact: Freshwater mussels help filter tiny particles from water as they feed.

subject: Dragonfly Nymph
fact: Dragonfly nymphs live underwater before changing into flying adults.

subject: Water Strider
fact: Water striders use surface tension to skate across the top of ponds and streams.
